title: Canada's January deliberations explain why Council kept both policy directions open
summary: The record of discussions leading to the Bank of Canada's 28 January decision explains how Governing Council could view 2.25% as stimulative relative to its estimated neutral range and still choose to wait. The economy had performed broadly as envisaged in October, with excess supply, moderating underlying inflation and some support for domestic demand. The risks around that baseline had increased, and several of them affected potential output as well as demand. Members explicitly found it unusually difficult to put probabilities on them. They could agree on the rate appropriate for the central projection while finding little basis to predict either the timing or the sign of its next change. The 11 February publication records the final stage of deliberations after staff briefings, with meetings beginning 20 January. It is evidence about the January decision.

The international backdrop contained a tension between strong financial conditions and fragile underlying assumptions. US household spending and AI investment had supported stronger-than-expected growth. Members expected equity wealth and productivity-driven real income gains to help consumption, while acknowledging softer hiring. Tariffs were raising prices. The increase was expected to fade, but businesses might have deferred price rises by selling previously acquired inventories. Running those down could prolong pass-through. Strong services and future fiscal spending supported Europe despite weak manufacturing. In China, export diversion and stimulus had helped deliver 5% growth in 2025, but weak housing and investment raised doubts about continued momentum. Council saw upside to growth from AI investment and a vulnerability if expected returns disappointed. Buoyant equities and tight credit spreads described prevailing conditions rather than an estimate of how much those assets would fall in that scenario (“International economy”).

Canada's quarterly GDP fluctuations were partly the result of swings in net exports and inventories induced by tariffs. Following strong third-quarter growth, Council expected fourth-quarter growth close to zero and a subsequent pickup. Reorganised supply chains, possible new trade agreements and stronger US demand could support exports, although the speed of adaptation was uncertain. Members distinguished resilient consumption from households' concerns about jobs and finances. Past rate cuts, higher equity prices and disposable income could sustain modest growth in per-person spending. Housing might recover unevenly because affordability remained a constraint around Toronto and Vancouver. Investment was weak beyond the industries immediately affected by tariffs and likely to remain soft for most of 2026. Federal and provincial infrastructure spending offered support, but its full effect would take time. Evidence that AI spending had raised Canadian productivity was still limited.

The unemployment rate had eased to 6.8% in December from 7.1% in August and September. Among younger workers, the decline was from 14.6% in September to 13.3% in December. Most recent employment gains were in services. Trade-exposed employment had stabilised after substantial losses earlier in the year and those losses had yet to spread widely, but few firms planned to hire. Members' assessment of a soft labour market drew on that breadth of evidence. The projection of 1.1% growth in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027 incorporated slower population growth, prolonged adjustment and gradual absorption of spare capacity (“Canadian economy and inflation outlook”).

Headline inflation at 2.4% reflected food and the tax-holiday base effect. CPI excluding indirect taxes eased to 2.5% in December. Preferred core measures eased from around 3% in October to about 2.5% in December, while their shorter three- and six-month measures were near or below 2%. Easing input and unit labour costs and limited reports of capacity constraints reinforced the inference that underlying pressures were cooling. Food and rent inflation remained concerns for households, however, and near-term consumer inflation expectations were somewhat elevated even as longer-term expectations softened. Members expected the cost of changing suppliers and trade routes to offset part of the disinflationary effect of excess supply.

The agreement review imposed a particularly difficult trade-off. Businesses could postpone capital spending until the terms of US market access became clearer. A broader set of tariffs would depress growth. Weaker demand could lower inflation, while more expensive imports, retaliation or disrupted supply chains could raise it. Diversifying exports might eventually support investment, but provided limited guidance about the immediate adjustment. Geopolitical strains and threats to Federal Reserve independence added uncertainty. Even within Canada the same observed weakness in output could have different policy implications depending on whether displaced capital and labour found new uses quickly or productive capacity suffered a lasting loss. Council therefore preserved the option to respond in either direction. The deliberations offer no probabilities, market pricing comparison or numerical trigger for action (“Considerations for monetary policy” and “Policy decision”).

questions.question: How much of weak Canadian output represents recoverable slack?
questions.detail: Council judges that excess supply exists but acknowledges substantial uncertainty about potential output as jobs and capital move across sectors. A larger permanent loss of capacity would reduce the scope for monetary easing even with weak GDP. Track industry-level utilisation, investment, hiring and wage growth alongside the Bank's estimates of capacity. Compare capacity expansion in gaining sectors with persistent displacement in industries losing US market access.

questions.question: Would a broader tariff shock reach prices before it reaches domestic demand?
questions.detail: The record describes both channels and highlights US inventories as a possible reason for delayed price responses. It gives no empirical sequence for Canada. Follow inventories and import unit values in exposed industries, subsequent producer and consumer prices, orders and household spending. The order in which those series move matters for near-term inflation exposure and for the short policy path consistent with a longer-run weakening of activity.

questions.question: What evidence would show that labour weakness is spreading beyond the initially affected sectors?
questions.detail: Recent service hiring and stabilisation in trade-exposed employment temper the aggregate unemployment signal, while forward hiring intentions remain weak. Compare employment, hours and vacancies across exposed manufacturers, their domestic suppliers and locally oriented services. Subsequent survey hiring plans and payroll outcomes would help distinguish delayed spillovers from an orderly reallocation. The distinction affects the durability of consumption in Council's projection.
